1401.title: Pride, the last thief
1401.hook: ahankar is the last and hardest thief
1401.howItsDone: Sikhs name ahankar, pride, among the five thieves and counter it with nimrata, humility, through Naam Simran and seva, such as cleaning shoes and serving langar in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger: the burning thief that pushes compassion out of its chair. Your line was breathe first.

A whole morning in the gurdwara shoe room. Rows of sneakers and sandals, wiped and set straight, handed back with a smile. Real seva, done well. Then the drive home, and a small thought slips into the passenger seat: not everyone would have done that. Nothing loud. Just a warm little glow, a quiet tally. The other thieves need some kind of opening. Anger needs an insult. Greed needs something shiny. This one walked in through the good deed itself. Today: pride, ahankar, the thief the title calls the last.
screen: `A MORNING OF SEVA IN THE SHOE ROOM.` → `NOT EVERYONE WOULD HAVE DONE THAT.` → `PRIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ahankar: pride, the swollen I, the self puffed up and asking to be seen. When the Granth names the five thieves, it lists them as lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Pride closes the list. Second, why it's the hardest. Every other thief can be fought, and the fighting itself can feed this one. Beat your anger and you can grow proud of your calm. Give up greed and you can grow proud of your simplicity. Even humility can turn into a trophy. That's one way to read the title: the last thief is the one still standing after you've beaten the others, because it lives on the beating. Third, the Guru's mirror. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says it in one sharp line, in paraphrase: whoever calls himself good, goodness does not come near him. Not, goodness leaves him. It never comes close. Fourth, the hope, in a salok you met early on this path. In Asa di Var, Guru Angad, the Second Guru, speaks of haumai, the ego under pride, in paraphrase: ego is a long, deep disease, but its cure is also within it. The same self that swells can bow. The Gurus' cure is grace and the Name, remembered again and again, and seva that's done and then forgotten. So the seva in the shoe room was good. The tally on the drive home is the thief. The way through isn't to stop serving. It's to catch the tally, smile at it, and hand the credit back to the One who gave the hands.
screen: `AHANKAR: THE SWOLLEN I.` · `IT FEEDS ON BEATING THE OTHERS.` · `CALL YOURSELF GOOD, GOODNESS STAYS AWAY.` · `THE CURE IS ALSO WITHIN.` · then, large: `THE LAST THIEF.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day or two for something you did well, then for the little glow that came after it, the quiet tally: at least I, not everyone would. Don't scold it; catch it gently, the way you'd lift a cat off the kitchen counter, and set it down. On each out-breath, hand the credit back, and if you pray, thank the Lord for the hands that did the work.
Pride. Ahankar, the swollen I, the thief that can feed even on victories over the others; the Gurus say its cure is also within. Today's word.
Your line: the last thief. The same self that swells can bow. Until tomorrow.

1402.title: Attachment, the clutching thief
1402.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of moh as one of the five thieves (panj chor) and seek to overcome it while living fully as householders, through remembrance of the Name and the Guru's teaching rather than by leaving family life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pride, ahankar, the thief that slips in last and answers to your own name. Your line was the last thief.

A small girl at the beach scoops up a fistful of wet sand. She loves it, so she squeezes, and the tighter she squeezes, the faster it runs out between her fingers. Her father, beside her, holds his sand in an open palm, and it just stays there, catching the light. Same sand, same love, different hands. The Gurus have a word for the closed fist: moh, attachment, and the Guru Granth Sahib names it among the thieves that live inside the body. This thief is slippery in its own way, because it looks so much like love.
screen: `A FISTFUL OF SAND.` → `THE OPEN PALM.` → `MOH: THE CLOSED FIST.`

segments.voice: First, the list. In a hymn by Guru Amar Das, in paraphrase: within this body live five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride; they plunder the nectar, and the self-willed don't even notice. Second, what moh is not. Sikhs live as householders, with families, jobs and kitchens, so moh can't mean loving your family, and the Gurus don't ask anyone to walk out on home to beat it. Guru Nanak names its reach in Rag Asa, in paraphrase: attachment to family, attachment to all our work; give up attachment, it is all corruption. Not the family. Not the work. The attachment: love that has turned into grip. This person must stay exactly as they are, this house, this job, this version of my life, or I can't breathe. Third, the open hand. In the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with yogis who had left the world behind, he gives them a picture of living inside it: as the lotus stays untouched in the water, as the duck swims through the stream, so the one who keeps the Word in mind crosses the world-ocean. The lotus is in the water. It just doesn't drown. Fourth, why it counts as a thief. Clutching steals the very thing it's guarding. The grip makes a friend feel watched, a grown child feel smothered, a good evening feel too small to enjoy because it might end. The love was real. The fist is what spoils it.
screen: `FIVE THIEVES IN THE BODY.` · `NOT THE FAMILY. THE GRIP.` · `THE LOTUS IN THE WATER.` · `CLUTCHING STEALS WHAT IT GUARDS.` · then, large: `HOLD, DON'T CLUTCH.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and bring to mind someone or something you love and are afraid to lose; let the fear be there. Then, breath by breath, picture that love resting in your open palm, the way the sand rested in the father's hand: not thrown away, not squeezed, held. If your fingers start to curl, let them open again, and if you pray, hold that person before God with open hands.
Attachment. Moh: love that clutches, named among the thieves in the Gurus' list. Not the love itself; the grip. Today's word.
Your line: hold, don't clutch. Like the lotus: in the water, and not drowning. See you tomorrow.

1403.title: Greed, the never-enough thief
1403.howItsDone: Sikhs count lobh, greed, among the five thieves; the Sikh answer is honest work (kirat), sharing (vand chhakna) and contentment, not renouncing money, and the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago is often told to make the point.

segments.voice: Yesterday, attachment, moh, the sand resting in an open palm. Your line was hold, don't clutch.

One more pair of shoes. One more thing in the cart. One more raise, and then life can relax. Greed rarely calls itself greed. It calls itself almost there. The finish line keeps sliding forward, and the runner pays for it in sleep, in worry, in evenings not spent with the people in the next room. Guru Nanak put his finger on this in the very first pauri of the Japji, the hymn Sikhs recite in the morning. Today's thief is lobh, the one that never says enough.

First, the hunger. In the opening pauri of the Japji, in paraphrase: the hunger of the hungry does not go away, even if they pile up loads of the world's goods. Bhukhiaa bhukh na utree. It isn't a threat; it's an observation. The pile grows, and the hunger stays exactly where it was. Second, an image that sticks. In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak lines up the vices as low company. In paraphrase: greed is a dog, falsehood is the sweeper, and cheating is eating carrion. Greed as a dog: nose down, always sniffing for the next scrap, never full, never off duty. Third, a story Sikhs tell. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say that in Saidpur he stayed with Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned his bread with his own hands. A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a grand feast and expected the Guru, who didn't come. Pressed for a reason, the story goes, he took Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's fine food in the other, and squeezed. From Lalo's bread came milk. From Bhago's, blood. Wealth wrung out of other people carries what it cost them. Fourth, the cure isn't poverty. Sikhs are taught to work hard, earn honestly and share. Lobh isn't having money. It's never letting any of it be enough, and never letting any of it go. The word that stops this thief is very small. Enough.
screen: `THE HUNGER THAT DOESN'T GO.` · `GREED IS A DOG.` · `LALO'S MILK, BHAGO'S BLOOD.` · `NOT POVERTY: ENOUGH.` · then, large: `ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you keep reaching for more of, money, likes, food, praise, hours at work, and just see it, without scolding yourself. On each breath out, let the single word enough be the whole sentence. Between breaths, notice what's already in your hands, a roof, a meal, a person, this breath, and if you pray, give thanks for one of them.
Greed. Lobh: the thief that never lets anything be enough, the dog that's never full. Today's word.
Your line: enough. One small word against a hunger that never fills. Same time tomorrow.

1404.title: Desire in its place
1404.hook: kaam: desire put in its place by discipline and love
1404.howItsDone: Sikhs count kaam among the five thieves and meet it not with celibacy but with married, faithful householder life, the discipline of the Sikh code of conduct and the remembrance of the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed, lobh, the dog that's never full, and the carpenter's bread that gave milk. Your line was enough.

Midnight, and the phone lights up. A dessert, a stranger's photo, an ad that seems to know exactly what to show. Desire is no stranger to human life. It gets people out of bed, into kitchens, into marriages, into music and art. The question the Gurus press isn't whether it's there. It's where it sits: in the passenger seat, or behind the wheel. Today's thief is kaam: desire, and above all the pull of lust. The Sikh answer isn't to kill it. It's to put it in its place.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AND THE PHONE LIGHTS UP.` → `PASSENGER SEAT OR STEERING WHEEL?` → `KAAM.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. Kaam opens the Gurus' list of thieves. In the same run of saloks that cried out to anger a few days ago, Guru Arjan turns to desire. In paraphrase: O desire, you lead people to hell and set them wandering from life to life; you steal the mind, you reach across the worlds, you tear apart meditation, discipline and good conduct. Strong language, and it's meant to be. Unruled, desire takes the wheel. Second, the householder. And yet the Sikh answer is not celibacy, and not a monastery. The Sikh path is a householder's path, and the Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, is a sacred rite: the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan, hymns of Guru Ram Das, are sung. Desire inside a faithful, committed love isn't a thief breaking in. It's family, living at home. Third, the discipline. The Sikh code of conduct asks for faithfulness in marriage, and in Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan describes a person of God as one whose eyes don't look on another's wife with desire. Restraint here isn't hatred of the body. It's keeping a promise, with the eyes as well as the hands. Fourth, love as the rein. Discipline alone is a fence, and fences get climbed. The Gurus pair it with love for the One, so the heart's deepest wanting has somewhere true to go. The pull doesn't vanish; it gets pointed. Desire in its place: not killed, not crowned. Kept.
screen: `GURU ARJAN'S WARNING.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH.` · `EYES THAT KEEP A PROMISE.` · `LOVE AS THE REIN.` · then, large: `NOT KILLED, NOT CROWNED. KEPT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one pull that tends to grab the wheel, a late-night scroll, a second helping, a look that lingers, a purchase at midnight, and name it gently, without shame: there you are. Picture the moment it's likely to show up, and see yourself pausing for one full breath and choosing, this once, not to follow it. If you pray, ask for steadiness in your own words.
Desire in its place. Kaam, desire and lust, ruled by discipline and pointed by love: in the Sikh answer, not killed and not crowned. Today's word.
Your line: desire in its place. A pull can wait a breath at the door. Until tomorrow.

1405.title: Chardi kala as philosophy
1405.hook: a settled optimism rooted in trust, not in circumstances
1405.howItsDone: Sikhs close the Ardas with the words 'Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala', and speak of chardi kala as a settled, rising spirit grounded in trust in Waheguru rather than in how things are going.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaam, desire in its place: not killed and not crowned, but kept. Your line was desire in its place.

The email that says no. The test result. The car that won't start in the rain. A setback lands, and there's a phrase for how Sikhs try to meet it, a phrase that closes the Ardas, the standing prayer: chardi kala. Rising spirits. It showed up early on this path as hope that keeps getting up. Today it isn't a mood. It's a way of seeing the world, with roots that go down below the weather.
screen: `A SETBACK LANDS.` → `CHARDI KALA.` → `NOT A MOOD: A PHILOSOPHY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The Ardas closes with these words: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. In paraphrase: Nanak, with the Name, rising spirits; by your will, the good of all. Look at what chardi kala stands next to. Not good news. Not a lucky break. Naam, the Name. The rising is rooted. Second, roots, not circumstances. Ordinary cheer climbs and falls with the forecast. Chardi kala, as Sikhs describe it, rests on trust in the One, so it doesn't need the forecast to cooperate. A tree on a windy hill bends hard in a storm. It stays because of what's underground. Third, it doesn't pretend. Earlier in this stretch, the Gurus called pain a medicine, without ever pretending it isn't pain. Chardi kala doesn't deny the setback. It simply refuses to let the setback write the ending. Grief and rising spirits can sit in the same person on the same afternoon. Fourth, it faces outward. The line doesn't end with my spirits. It ends with sarbat da bhala, the good of all. In Sikh thought, rising spirits are meant to be shared. The one in chardi kala can be the one others lean on in a hard room: steady voice, warm tea, a joke at the right moment. Not because things are fine. Because the roots hold.
screen: `NAAM, THEN CHARDI KALA.` · `ROOTS, NOT THE FORECAST.` · `IT DOESN'T PRETEND.` · `RISING FOR THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `RISING, ROOTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one setback from this week, small or not so small, and notice where it sits in your body. Breathe in and picture roots going down from where you sit, into ground the setback can't reach; breathe out and let the corners of your mouth lift a little, not because it's fine, but because you're still standing. If you pray, say the Ardas's closing words quietly: Nanak naam chardi kala.
Chardi kala as philosophy. Rising spirits, rooted in the Name and in trust, not in circumstances, and turned toward the good of all. Today's word.
Your line: rising, rooted. Bent by the storm, held by what's underground. See you tomorrow.

1406.title: Acceptance and rising spirits
1406.hook: bhaana and chardi kala belong together
1406.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of living in bhaana, God's will, while keeping chardi kala, rising spirits; the two are joined in the closing words of the Ardas, and the Japji's refrain 'jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar' voices the acceptance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala as philosophy: the tree on the windy hill, held by its roots. Your line was rising, rooted.

Bow your head, or lift it? Some people hear acceptance and think of giving up. Some hear rising spirits and think of fighting fate. Two words have walked through this stretch of the path: bhaana, the will, the sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends, and chardi kala, rising spirits. Side by side, they can look like opposites. One bows; the other lifts. The Sikh tradition doesn't choose between them. It says them in a single breath, at the very end of the Ardas.

First, the line. Yesterday's words again: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Rising spirits, and then, by your will, the good of all. Rising and accepting share one sentence, and neither cancels the other. Second, a refrain. In the Japji, Guru Nanak stops at the end of a pauri, overwhelmed by the size of creation, and says, in paraphrase: whatever pleases you, that alone is good; you are forever whole, formless One. Jo tudh bhaavai saaee bhalee kaar. The next pauri ends with the same words, and the next. Acceptance there isn't one grim moment; it's a line the Japji keeps coming back to. Third, what acceptance isn't. Bhaana doesn't mean liking injustice or sitting still. The same people who recite that refrain every morning run free kitchens and stand up to wrong. Acceptance is about the ground under your feet: this happened. Rising is about the next step: and now. Fourth, the hinge. Accept first, so your strength stops pouring into fighting what already is. Then rise, so it can pour into what can still be done. A farmer wakes to find hail has flattened the field. Bhaana says: it happened, and it's in the Lord's hands. Chardi kala says: there's seed in the shed. Grieve the field. Then replant.

1407.title: Asking and accepting
1407.hook: Ardas both asks and then accepts the answer
1407.howItsDone: Sikhs offer Ardas standing with joined hands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the close of services and before important tasks; afterward a hukamnama is read from the Granth and received as the Guru's word for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farmer who grieves the hail, then replants: acceptance and rising spirits in one breath. Your line was accept, then rise.

The end of a gurdwara service. Everyone stands, hands joined, faces turned toward the Guru Granth Sahib, and one person leads the Ardas, the standing petition, while the sangat listens. Names are spoken: someone in the hospital, a new baby, a family about to travel, a student with an exam. Then the asking ends, everyone bows, and a reading is taken from the Granth, the hukamnama, received as the Guru's word for the day. First the asking. Then the listening.

First, Ardas really asks. It names needs and sorrows, journeys and exams, the sick and the grieving, and it ends by asking for the good of all. Sikhs aren't asked to pretend they need nothing. Second, it asks humbly. Near the close, the one leading asks forgiveness for any mistakes made, bhul chuk, even in the prayer itself. And some sangats recite a verse from Guru Arjan's Sukhmani Sahib just before the Ardas. In paraphrase: you are the master, to you this prayer; body and soul are your gift; you are mother and father, we are your children. The one asking stands like a child before a parent, not a customer at a counter. Third, it accepts. The prayer ends with the will: tere bhaane sarbat da bhala, by your will, the good of all. Then the hukam is read and received as the Guru's word, whatever it says. Two open hands: lifted up to ask, and left open for whatever comes down. Fourth, a look back. This week the thieves came through one by one: pride, attachment, greed, desire. Then chardi kala, rising spirits rooted in the Name, and acceptance and rising together. And now the Ardas, which holds all of it. The thieves grab. The Ardas asks, and then lets go.
